Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "hey, could you help me turn the notes below into catalogue entries for the next section of our family photo catalogue? this is the Bell family archive, including relatives who married into the Ortega family. My mother Lena Bell scanned this batch in 2024 from an album that had been kept in a drawer at Ruth Bell’s house in Eugene, Oregon. The album has “summer and other days” written inside the front cover. Please work with the twelve image files BELL_041 through BELL_052, in that order. The scan order follows the album pages, so keep it even where the dates jump around. I want entries that someone outside the family can understand, but they should still sound like catalogue records rather than little stories or guesses.

The older spreadsheet, started by my aunt June in 2019, has columns for file name, date or date range, people, place, and description. Keep those fields, and add a separate source note when it helps distinguish what is visible in the photograph from what someone later wrote or remembered. One entry per image, please. Put the file name first and use the same order as the scans. Dates can be approximate when the supplied notes support that, but don’t turn a possibility into a firm date. If the notes don’t establish something, say that it is not identified or leave it undated rather than filling it in from family knowledge that isn’t included here.

For BELL_041, there are two adults standing on a porch. A pencil note on the album page identifies the woman as Ruth Bell; it does not name the man. There is no date written beside the picture. A note in the spreadsheet puts this group of pages around 1970–72, but it doesn’t explain how that range was decided. BELL_042 shows three children by a backyard sprinkler. The album note names them Nora, Peter, and Eli, and says “Eugene, summer 1972.” Please retain the names as written, without trying to add surnames. BELL_043 shows a woman seated at a table with a cake. June’s handwritten label says “June’s 40th,” but no year or place is given. Don’t calculate her birthday or infer where the gathering was held.

BELL_044 is a view from inside a car, with the road and a blue station wagon visible through the window; no people can be identified. On the back of the print is the note “near Bend, maybe 1973.” Keep “maybe” attached to the date and place information. BELL_045 shows two women beside a picnic table. Lena’s scanning notes identify one as Ruth and say the other may be her sister-in-law, but there is no name for that person. The picnic appears to be at a lake, though the lake is not identified. BELL_046 is a close view of a hand holding a small paper ticket. The ticket text is too faint to read in the scan. The album page has no note for this image, so a plain visual description is enough; don’t guess what event the ticket was for.

BELL_047 shows a group in front of a cabin. A note added by David Bell in 2021 names Ruth, June, and “the Ortega cousins,” but doesn’t identify the cousins individually. It also says “first trip together, I think.” Keep that wording as a recollection, not as a confirmed description of what happened. BELL_048 is a child standing beside a bicycle in a driveway. The name “Mara” is written underneath the image, with no surname or date. BELL_049 shows four people carrying folding chairs toward a covered picnic area. There are no names or place notes. BELL_050 shows a dog on a porch step; the album label reads “Scout,” with no indication of whose dog it was. BELL_051 is an indoor group photograph with six people, but only June and Ruth are identified in a note. BELL_052 shows a stack of dishes and serving bowls after what may have been a meal. The note says “after everyone left,” but gives no date, place, or names.

Keep descriptions brief but specific enough to distinguish the images. State visible details separately from information supplied by album labels, the spreadsheet, or later notes. Don’t identify people from appearance alone, and don’t fill in relationships beyond what these notes say. Use neutral language for unknown people and places. The family uses “Aunt June” in conversation, but in the catalogue use June unless a source actually gives a fuller name. Please don’t combine similar-looking pictures into one entry or omit an image just because it has little identifying information.

There is one family recollection that may be useful when you get to the vehicle and trip photographs. In an email about this album, David wrote, “I think this was the first summer we had the blue station wagon.” The email doesn’t say which photograph he meant. You can include this as a source note for the relevant image or images only if the connection is clear from the supplied details; if it isn’t clear, leave it out rather than assigning it to a particular scene. The current review covers all twelve files, but the question we are trying to assess most carefully is whether the notes for BELL_047–BELL_052 support any additional names, dates, or trip details beyond those already stated. Keep that assessment within those six records and the evidence supplied here; don’t turn a remembered phrase into confirmation, and don’t make a conclusion about the whole album.", "output": "Create catalogue entries for the twelve family photographs in the Bell family archive, including relatives who married into the Ortega family. The photographs are files BELL_041 through BELL_052. They were scanned by Lena Bell in 2024 from an album kept in a drawer at Ruth Bell’s house in Eugene, Oregon. The album has “summer and other days” written inside its front cover. Use the scan order, which follows the album pages, even when dates vary.

Write one entry per image, in file-name order. Keep the existing spreadsheet fields: file name, date or date range, people, place, and description. Add a separate source note where needed to distinguish visible details from information written or remembered later. Make each description brief but specific enough to distinguish its photograph, and understandable to readers outside the family. Use the supplied notes only: do not infer identities, dates, places, or relationships. Dates may be approximate when supported by the notes; retain uncertainty where stated. If the information is not established, leave it undated or unidentified rather than filling gaps with outside family knowledge. Use neutral wording for unknown people and places. Use “June” in the catalogue unless a source gives a fuller name.

Use these image-specific notes:

1. **BELL_041:** Two adults standing on a porch. A pencil note on the album page identifies the woman as Ruth Bell but does not name the man. No date is written beside the photograph. The spreadsheet places this group of pages around 1970–72 but does not explain the basis for that range.
2. **BELL_042:** Three children beside a backyard sprinkler. The album note names them Nora, Peter, and Eli and says “Eugene, summer 1972.” Retain the names as written; do not add surnames.
3. **BELL_043:** A woman seated at a table with a cake. June’s handwritten label says “June’s 40th.” No year or place is given; do not calculate a birthday or infer a location.
4. **BELL_044:** A view from inside a car, with the road and a blue station wagon visible through the window. No people can be identified. The back of the print says “near Bend, maybe 1973.” Preserve the uncertainty in “maybe” for both the date and place information.
5. **BELL_045:** Two women beside a picnic table. Lena’s scanning notes identify one as Ruth and say the other may be her sister-in-law, without naming her. The setting appears to be a lake, but the lake is unidentified.
6. **BELL_046:** A close view of a hand holding a small paper ticket. Its text is too faint to read in the scan, and the album page has no note. Give a visual description only; do not guess the event.
7. **BELL_047:** A group in front of a cabin. A note David Bell added in 2021 names Ruth, June, and “the Ortega cousins,” without identifying the cousins individually. The note also says “first trip together, I think.” Treat this as a recollection, not a confirmed account.
8. **BELL_048:** A child beside a bicycle in a driveway. “Mara” is written underneath the image; no surname or date is supplied.
9. **BELL_049:** Four people carrying folding chairs toward a covered picnic area. No names or place notes are supplied.
10. **BELL_050:** A dog on a porch step. The album label reads “Scout,” but does not say whose dog it was.
11. **BELL_051:** An indoor group photograph of six people. A note identifies only June and Ruth.
12. **BELL_052:** A stack of dishes and serving bowls after what may have been a meal. The note says “after everyone left,” with no date, place, or names.

Do not combine similar-looking photographs or omit images with little identifying information. Keep visible details separate from information supplied by album labels, the spreadsheet, or later notes. Do not extend the stated relationships or identify people from appearance alone.

David wrote in an email about the album, “I think this was the first summer we had the blue station wagon.” The email does not identify a photograph. Include the recollection as a source note for a vehicle or trip image only if its connection is clear from the supplied details; otherwise, leave it out rather than assigning it to a scene. The review covers all twelve files, with particular attention to whether the notes for BELL_047–BELL_052 support any additional names, dates, or trip details. Keep that assessment to those six records and the evidence provided. Do not treat a remembered phrase as confirmation or draw a conclusion about the whole album."}]
